supported_cases.query: What is a process address space?

claims.text: A process is a program in execution, and each process has its own address space. The operating system saves the process state in a process control block during a context switch.
Threads within the same process share code, data, and open files. Each thread has its own stack and registers. Threads provide concurrent execution within one address space.
Threads within the same process share code, data, and open files.
Each thread has its own stack and registers, meaning these are not shared among threads in the same process.
Threads provide concurrent execution within one address space.
Deadlock occurs when a set of processes waits forever for resources held by another member of the set.
The four necessary deadlock conditions are: mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, and circular wait.
In round robin scheduling, each ready process is given a fixed time quantum to execute on the CPU.
When a process's time quantum expires, that running process is moved to the back of the ready queue, allowing the next process in line to run.
In First Come First Served (FCFS) scheduling, ready processes are executed in the order they arrive.
The convoy effect is caused by a long CPU burst that delays shorter jobs behind it in the FCFS queue, so all subsequent short jobs must wait for the long job to finish before they can run.

supported_cases.query: How does a mutex protect a critical section?

claims.text: A mutex protects a critical section by allowing only one thread to enter at a time.
A race condition occurs when the result depends on the interleaving of concurrent accesses to shared data, which is the problem a mutex prevents in a critical section.
